summary: Defines a set of metrics and their use for evaluating the end-to-end performance of SIP telephony services in production and testing, so measurements can be compared across implementations.

eli5.summary: Phone systems need a shared way to measure how well calls are set up. This lists the measurements so different companies can compare their results.

subtitle: Nine standard ways to measure how quickly and how often SIP phone registrations, call setups and hang-ups work.

tldr.problem: Many standards measure telephony signaling such as SS7, but none of the metrics specifically address SIP, so operators and vendors could not compare SIP performance on a common footing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines nine metrics (delays, durations and ratios) computed from identifiable SIP messages such as REGISTER, INVITE, 200 OK and BYE, together with rules for clocks and time stamps (t1 and t4).
tldr.outcome: Operators, vendors and users get a shared vocabulary for production and test measurements, but the RFC deliberately sets no numeric targets or thresholds.

facts.label: Metrics defined
facts.value: 9 (RRD, IRA, SRD, SDD, SDT, SER, SEER, ISA, SCR)

facts.label: Clock error limit
facts.value: Less than +/- 1 ms for the t4-t1 interval

today: RFC 6076 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2011, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the RFC that defines these SIP telephony metrics.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
SIP is widely used by service providers, vendors and end users in telecommunications. Other standards measure telephony signaling such as Signaling System 7 (SS7), but none of those metrics specifically address SIP. RFC 6076 defines a standard set of metrics for measuring and reporting end-to-end SIP performance in a telephony environment. Its intended audience is network operators, who often collect information on how responsive the network is to customer requests.

The scope is narrow on purpose. The metrics do not consider failure or impairment of the application processing of a request, and they do not separate application processing time from other delay such as packet transfer delay. Metrics for a single device's processing performance are out of scope. The RFC also gives no numerical objectives or acceptance thresholds, because these are beyond the scope of IETF activities in general.

The metrics work with dedicated test messages (active measurement) or with user-initiated traffic on a live network (passive measurement).
sections.eli5: It is a rulebook for timing and counting phone calls in the same way everywhere. It does not say what a good score is, only how to measure it.

sections.title: Terms and Clock Rules
sections.content:
The RFC treats end-to-end as the originating user agent client (UAC), the destination user agent server (UAS) and any interim proxies, possibly including back-to-back user agents (B2BUAs). A session is identified by a unique Call-ID plus the To and From tags. Session establishment happens when a 200 OK from the target is received in response to the originating INVITE. The metrics measure signaling only, even where their names include the word session.

Each interval is bounded by two instants. t1 is the start time: the first bit of the request has been sent and is externally observable. t4 is the end time: the last bit of the designated response has been received by the SIP application. The names t2 and t3 are reserved for future use at another interface. In the metrics, t1 is not reset when the same message is retransmitted within the same transaction.

Clock quality matters. The clock supplying t1 SHOULD be synchronized to a primary time source such as UTC, clocks at different measurement points SHOULD be synchronized to each other, and the clock offset and relative offset MUST be reported with each measurement. The error in the t4 minus t1 interval SHOULD be constrained to less than +/- 1 ms. Clock correction SHOULD be suspended during a measurement interval, unless that accuracy is still met.
sections.eli5: Start the stopwatch when the first bit of your message leaves, and stop it when the last bit of the answer arrives. Everybody must also keep their watches set to the same time and say how accurate their watch is.

sections.title: Registration and Setup Metrics
sections.content:
Three metrics cover registering a phone and starting a session. Registration Request Delay (RRD) is the time from the first bit of the initial REGISTER to the last bit of the 200 OK, including the expected authentication challenge. It is reported only for successful registrations, in milliseconds. Ineffective Registration Attempts (IRA) is the percentage of REGISTER requests that end in a final failure: a 4XX (excluding the 401, 402 and 407 challenge codes), a 5XX, a possible 6XX, or a Timer F expiry. Only the first REGISTER of a transaction counts; retries with the same topmost Via branch value MUST be ignored.

Session Request Delay (SRD) is the time from the INVITE to the first status-indicating response, normally the first provisional response that is not 100 Trying (a 200 is used if it arrives first). It is measured at the originating UA only and SHOULD be stated in seconds. SRD for failed requests MUST NOT be combined with SRD for successful ones, and the output MUST say which it is. If the INVITE is redirected with a 3XX, the interval spans the redirect. The RFC notes that SRD is similar to Post-Selection Delay in ITU-T E.721.

Because authentication is part of registration and setup, networks mixing Digest with other mechanisms such as Identity are likely to see a multimodal RRD distribution.
sections.eli5: Three stopwatches: one for how long signing in to the phone network takes, one for how often signing in fails, and one for how long you wait before the other phone starts ringing.

sections.title: Ending and Lasting Metrics
sections.content:
Session Disconnect Delay (SDD) runs from sending a completion message such as BYE to receiving the 2XX response. It can be measured at either end and SHOULD be stated in milliseconds. Disconnects that fail MUST NOT be combined with successful ones. A recoverable error such as 503 Retry-After is not used as the end time; the 2XX of the recovery is used. If no response ever comes and Timer F expires, the session SHOULD be excluded.

Session Duration Time (SDT) runs from the 200 OK to an INVITE until the BYE (or a timeout), and is reported as an average in seconds. It is similar to Call Hold Time, traditionally computed as Average Call Hold Time (ACHT), and is meant to reveal problems such as poor audio quality that cause short sessions. It does not cover sessions that use only early media, for example an automated system that answers with a 183 Session Progress and ends with a CANCEL. At the target UA the interval starts when the 200 OK is sent. A failed completion ends at the Timer F expiry, and values measured at the two UAs can then differ by up to the value of Timer F.
sections.eli5: One stopwatch times how long hanging up takes. Another times how long the call lasted, and very short calls are a clue that something sounded bad.

sections.title: The Ratio Metrics
sections.content:
Four metrics are percentages, and each is undefined when its denominator is 0.

  • SER (Session Establishment Ratio): INVITEs with a 200 OK, divided by all INVITEs minus those answered with a 3XX, times 100. It is similar to Answer Seizure Ratio in ITU-T E.411.
  • SEER (Session Establishment Effectiveness Ratio): like SER, but the numerator also counts INVITEs ending in 480, 486, 600 or 603, which clearly reflect an individual user's behavior rather than the provider. It is similar to Network Effectiveness Ratio in E.411. Codes such as 401, 407 and 420 are deliberately left out of the numerator.
  • ISA (Ineffective Session Attempts): the percentage of session requests released internally with a failed or overloaded condition. The guideline set is 408, 500, 503 and 504. The metric was adopted from Telcordia GR-512-CORE.
  • SCR (Session Completion Ratio): sessions that complete without failing from lack of response, divided by total session requests, times 100. It is similar to Call Completion Ratio.

SER and SEER are measured at the originating UA only. The RFC suggests larger sample sets give a better indication. The sample period is left to the operator, for example hourly, daily, weekly or monthly.
sections.eli5: These count how many calls worked out of how many were tried, like a basketball shooting percentage. SEER does not blame the phone company when the person simply said no or was busy.

sections.title: Practical Considerations
sections.content:
Several factors change how the numbers are collected. A B2BUA can break the end-to-end view, because it may act as an originating UAC and terminating UAS or as a proxy, so data from both sides may be needed. Forking SHOULD be considered, since using every forked dialog would skew results; tags are used to tell dialogs apart, and an SRD measurement should be taken for each early or confirmed dialog created.

Authentication adds to the measured durations, and its failures are captured by the metrics. Inputs may come from call detail records, from raw signaling, from SNMP, from extensions to the SIP MIB, or from a possible new event package retrieved with SUBSCRIBE. If elements calculate the metrics themselves with different sample sizes, results for the same event can differ a lot. In a test environment, the setup MUST be documented accurately so results can be reproduced. The metrics can also be broken down by user or domain, in each direction.
sections.eli5: Real phone networks have tricky parts, like one call ringing many phones at once. The rules say how to count those fairly and to write down exactly how a test was done.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The data used as input to these calculations should itself be secured. All other security aspects follow RFC 3261. Implementers MUST also realize that the metrics could describe customer and user usage patterns, so privacy should be considered when collecting, transporting and storing them.

The RFC expects the metrics to be used in production telephony SIP environments as input for Key Performance Indicators (KPI) and Service Level Agreement (SLA) indications, and also for testing end-to-end SIP-based services.
sections.eli5: Call statistics can reveal when and how people use their phones, so keep the numbers safe and private.

viz.caption: THE RATIO METRICS AT A GLANCE

items.label: Session Establishment Ratio
items.desc: INVITEs with 200 OK over INVITEs less those with 3XX.

items.label: Session Establishment Effectiveness Ratio
items.desc: Also counts 480, 486, 600 and 603 in the numerator.

items.label: Ineffective Session Attempts
items.desc: Guideline codes 408, 500, 503 and 504 over total session requests.

items.label: Session Completion Ratio
items.desc: Successfully completed sessions over total session requests.
